documents.title: Queuelet: system context explained
documents.plain: Producers submit JSON jobs to named queues inside a namespace. Worker clients lease jobs, execute them outside Queuelet and report success or failure. Operators manage queues, jobs and schedules and inspect events and stats. Queuelet sends terminal-state notifications to a configured webhook receiver. In the lab that receiver is hooksink, a fault-controllable fake. Open Queuelet to see its containers. This is the explored and fixed b6df7db snapshot; its project tree is identical to the merged end-review fix pass (7d26bb8). It is not a claim of complete exploration or exactly-once execution.

ste.text: The producer sends jobs to Queuelet. A worker leases and executes jobs. The operator manages queues and jobs. Queuelet sends terminal notifications to a receiver. Delivery can repeat. Open Queuelet to see the containers.

documents.title: Queuelet: containers explained
documents.plain: The Go API owns queue state in PostgreSQL. Workers are separate clients: the API grants leases, but does not execute job payloads. qctl is a CLI used by producers and operators; its worker-run mode uses the same worker implementation. It is not a Compose service. The webhook receiver is an external collaborator; hooksink is its concrete lab fake, not a second production destination. The two outgoing notification arrows distinguish the general contract from the lab realization. PostgreSQL holds jobs, attempts, schedules, retained event history and notification snapshots. The service box holds what runs as the Queuelet service: the API and its PostgreSQL database. Worker, qctl and hooksink are Queuelet containers drawn outside that box because they are clients and a lab fake that run outside the service. Grey marks supporting elements: PostgreSQL, worker and qctl are supporting context outside the focused process in the API component view, and hooksink is a lab fake. Open Queue API for its in-process responsibilities.

ste.text: The API stores state in PostgreSQL. Workers and qctl use HTTP and bearer keys. Workers execute jobs outside the API. The API sends signed notifications. The lab uses hooksink as the receiver. The service box contains the API and PostgreSQL. Workers, qctl and hooksink operate outside the service.

documents.title: Queuelet: API components explained
documents.plain: All eight components run inside the Go API process. The core lifecycle goroutine promotes due work, expires leases, fires schedules and applies retention on a real one-second tick. Schedule firing is a function in that loop, not another service. A separate shipper goroutine processes at most 20 due outbox rows concurrently, with two-second HTTP timeouts; it does not block the core sweep on a slow receiver. The semantic clock supplies job and schedule times; only lab configuration exposes admin clock control. Real tickers and network deadlines do not freeze with it. The store component denotes the shared SQL pool and helpers; packages also use Store.DB directly. Events come from committed database history; logging and stats observe transitions rather than drive them. Auth checks hashed bearer keys and scopes handlers to namespaces. Admin is not universal job access: it has cross-namespace stats and lab clock privileges.

ste.text: These components run in one API process. The core loop runs lifecycle tasks. A separate loop sends notifications. The clock supplies semantic time. Real timers continue. SQL stores state. Events and stats observe committed changes.

documents.title: Queuelet: job lifecycle and notification flow explained
documents.plain: Read the numbered scenario as a successful enqueue → lease → execute → ack path followed by explicitly labelled alternatives. It is not a trace in which ack, nack, expiry and cancel all happen. Execution occurs in the worker between the lease reply and completion request. Heartbeats can extend an unexpired current lease; a matching cancelled lease reports cancellation and the sample worker stops cooperatively. Cancellation is immediately terminal, with late ack/nack rejected. Nack leads to retry_wait or dead when retries are refused, exhausted or the leased job was purged. Expiry or worker deletion consumes an attempt and returns work to queued or dead. Only dead work accepts operator retry; it resets attempts. scheduled and retry_wait promote when due. Terminal success/death/cancel records its notification in the same transaction as the transition, using a snapshot of destination, secret and body. A separate shipper reads it, signs the actual transmitted bytes and retries failures after five semantic seconds. The real one-second shipper ticker and two-second HTTP deadline still apply. A receiver can act and lose its reply, causing duplicate delivery. Execution and notification are not exactly-once. The state table is documentation/code, not another C4 view: scheduled/retry_wait → queued → leased; leased → succeeded/retry_wait/dead; active states → cancelled; dead → queued by operator retry. Retention deletes succeeded/cancelled, while dead letters persist.

ste.text: Enqueue a job, then lease it. The worker executes the job and sends ack or nack. Expiry, cancellation and retry are alternative paths. A terminal change and its notification commit together. A separate loop sends the notification. Delivery and execution can repeat.

documents.title: Queuelet: Compose lab deployment explained
documents.plain: Compose starts api, postgres, worker-a on emails, worker-b on reports, and hooksink. PostgreSQL data lives in a named volume. API :8200, sink :8201 and database :5432 publish to host defaults 18200, 18201 and 15433; ports can be overridden. Workers use api:8200 on the Compose network. The seeded reports queue points to hooksink:8201; webhook destination is per-queue configuration, not a fixed API deployment address. qctl and probe scripts are host clients or commands run with docker compose exec, not declared services. They inspect state, change sink modes and control semantic time. QUEUELET_TEST_CLOCK=1 is lab configuration: there is no clock container. Scheduler, sweeper, shipper and event logger all remain inside api. API and Postgres use unless-stopped restart; workers use on-failure; hooksink has no restart policy specified. This local teaching lab does not define production hosting or security.

ste.text: The lab runs API, PostgreSQL, two workers and a fake receiver. PostgreSQL uses a persistent volume. qctl and probes run outside the service list. The API test clock is enabled. The scheduler and shipper run inside API.
